sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 74 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: Remember Your congregation
study.intro: Asaph laments over the ruined sanctuary, asks God how long the enemy will mock His name, and then recalls God's ancient power over sea, day and night, pleading that God would rise and defend His afflicted people.
study.context: Psalm 74 is a Maskil, a teaching psalm, headed 'of Asaph'. It describes the temple burned and every meeting place destroyed, which most readers connect with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9), so 'of Asaph' likely points to the Asaphite guild of singers who carried on his name. Like Lamentations, it gives words to a community whose center of worship is gone. The psalm moves from complaint (1–11) to remembering God as Creator and King (12–17) and then to urgent petition (18–23).
study.peopleNote: The heading names Asaph, the Levite worship leader whose family of singers continued long after him; the app has no Asaph profile yet, so no person card is linked. The enemies are invading soldiers, not named individuals. Planned paintings would show ruined stone walls, scattered villagers and landscapes; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Why rejected forever
verses.heading: Smoke over the pasture
verses.meaning: The psalm begins 'A Maskil of Asaph' and opens with two raw questions: 'Why have You rejected us forever, O God? Why does Your anger smolder against the sheep of Your pasture?' The word 'smolder' pictures smoke rising, fitting for a psalm about a burned temple. Yet even in the complaint the people call themselves 'the sheep of Your pasture.' They still believe they belong to the Shepherd, which is exactly why His silence hurts so much. Lament is not unbelief; it is faith speaking honestly to God.
verses.context: A Maskil is a psalm meant to give insight. The image of Israel as God's flock appears in Psalm 79:13 and Psalm 95:7. Lamentations 5:20 asks the same question: 'Why do You forget us forever?'
explore: Maskil
A Hebrew heading that probably means a skillful or instructive psalm, one meant to teach as well as to be sung.
Smolder
To burn slowly with smoke; here a picture of God's anger lingering like a fire that will not go out.
verses.reflect: When have you felt that God had stepped away, and how can you still speak to Him as His own?
verses.alt: Smoke drifts over an empty hillside pasture beneath gray clouds.

verses.title: Purchased long ago
verses.heading: A people bought and kept
verses.meaning: Verse 2 asks God to 'remember Your congregation, which You purchased long ago and redeemed as the tribe of Your inheritance—Mount Zion, where You dwell.' The prayer appeals to God's own past actions. He bought this people out of Egypt; He chose Zion as His home. Asaph argues that God's investment in His people is a reason for Him to act again. When we pray, we can remind ourselves of what God has already done, because His past faithfulness is the ground of our present hope.
verses.context: Exodus 15:16 calls Israel 'the people You have bought.' Deuteronomy 32:9 says 'the LORD's portion is His people.' The New Testament speaks of believers bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20).
explore: Redeem
To buy back or set free by paying a price, as a relative might buy back land or free a family member.
Inheritance
A treasured possession passed down and kept; Israel is described as God's own inheritance among the nations.
verses.reflect: What has God already done for you that you can bring before Him when you pray today?
verses.alt: A hilltop city of stone houses glows in early light above terraced slopes.

verses.title: Everlasting ruins
verses.heading: Walk through the wreckage
verses.meaning: Verse 3 invites God to come and look: 'Turn Your steps to the everlasting ruins, to everything in the sanctuary the enemy has destroyed.' The ruins seem permanent, as if they will never be rebuilt. Asaph asks God to walk among the rubble, as a friend might be invited to see the damage after a disaster. It is a bold, personal request. It shows that we can bring God into the very places where our lives look broken beyond repair and ask Him to see them with us.
verses.context: Nehemiah 2:17 describes Jerusalem 'lying in ruins' with its gates burned. Isaiah 61:4 promises that God's people 'will rebuild the ancient ruins.' Lamentations 2:7 says the Lord rejected His altar and abandoned His sanctuary.
explore: Ruins
Collapsed walls and broken buildings; here the remains of the temple after the enemy destroyed it.
Sanctuary
A holy place set apart for meeting God; in Israel this was the tabernacle and later the temple in Jerusalem.
verses.reflect: Which ruined place in your life would you like to invite God to walk through with you?
verses.alt: Broken stone walls and fallen columns lie scattered on a quiet hill.

verses.title: Roaring foes
verses.heading: Banners in the holy place
verses.meaning: Verse 4 says, 'Your foes have roared within Your meeting place; they have unfurled their banners as signs.' Where praise once rose, enemy soldiers now shout like lions. Their military standards stand where God's signs and festivals used to be. The picture is of total reversal: the place for meeting God has become a camp for His enemies. The pain is not only loss of a building but the sense that God's honor is being trampled in public.
verses.context: Armies raised banners to mark conquered ground. Lamentations 2:7 says the enemy 'raised a shout in the house of the LORD as on a feast day.' Psalm 79:1 laments that 'the nations have invaded Your inheritance.'
explore: Meeting place
The appointed place where God met with His people, especially for worship and the yearly festivals.
Banners
Military flags or standards raised by an army to declare ownership of captured territory.
verses.reflect: Where do you see God's honor being mocked today, and how might you pray about it?
verses.alt: Foreign war banners flap above a stone courtyard under a stormy sky.

verses.title: Axes in a thicket
verses.heading: Like woodcutters gone wild
verses.meaning: Verse 5 compares the invaders to 'men wielding axes in a thicket of trees.' A woodcutter swings without care for what he cuts down; he simply clears the ground. The enemy treats the beautiful sanctuary like a tangle of brush to be hacked away. The image shows careless violence toward something precious. What took generations of skill and devotion to build was cut down in a short, thoughtless rage.
verses.context: Solomon's temple was paneled with cedar from Lebanon (1 Kings 6:15). Jeremiah 46:22 pictures invaders coming 'with axes, like woodcutters.' The comparison would remind hearers of forests felled by armies.
explore: Thicket
A dense growth of shrubs and small trees, usually cleared by cutting rather than shaped with care.
Cedar paneling
The fragrant, costly wood that lined the inner walls of Solomon's temple and was carved with decoration.
verses.reflect: What precious thing in your life needs protecting from careless or hurried damage?
verses.alt: Axes lie beside freshly cut stumps at the edge of a dark grove.

verses.title: Smashed carvings
verses.heading: Beauty broken with picks
verses.meaning: Verse 6 finishes the picture: they were 'smashing all the carvings with hatchets and picks.' The temple walls were carved with flowers, palm trees and cherubim, signs of the garden of God. Now the decorations lie in splinters. Asaph names the detail because grief often lingers on small, specific losses. God welcomes that kind of specific sorrow; we do not have to pretend that broken beauty does not matter.
verses.context: 1 Kings 6:29 says Solomon carved 'cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers' on the temple walls. These images echoed Eden. 2 Kings 25:13 records the Babylonians breaking up the bronze furnishings.
explore: Carvings
Decorative designs cut into wood or stone; the temple's carvings showed cherubim, palms and blossoms.
Cherubim
Heavenly guardian beings associated with God's presence, carved on the temple walls and on the ark's cover.
verses.reflect: What specific loss are you still grieving, and have you told God about it plainly?
verses.alt: Splintered pieces of carved wood with palm patterns lie on a stone floor.

verses.title: Burned to the ground
verses.heading: The dwelling of His Name
verses.meaning: Verse 7 states the worst: 'They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground; they have defiled the dwelling place of Your Name.' God had chosen to place His Name in the temple, the sign of His presence among His people. To burn it was to attack Him openly. Asaph does not soften the facts. Yet later Scripture shows that God's presence was never limited to a building; He would dwell among His people in new ways.
verses.context: 2 Kings 25:9 records that Nebuzaradan 'burned the house of the LORD.' Deuteronomy 12:11 speaks of the place God would choose 'as a dwelling for His Name.' John 1:14 says the Word 'dwelt among us.'
explore: His Name
God's revealed character and presence; placing His Name in the temple meant He chose to be known and met there.
Defile
To make something unclean or treat it as common, stripping it of the honor it should have.
verses.reflect: How does it help you to know God's presence is not confined to one place or building?
verses.alt: Charred beams and blackened stones smoke on a hill at sunset.

verses.title: Crush them completely
verses.heading: Every meeting place burned
verses.meaning: Verse 8 reveals the enemy's goal: 'They said in their hearts, “We will crush them completely.” They burned down every place where God met us in the land.' The plan was not just to win a battle but to erase a people and their worship. Every gathering place was targeted. This is the pattern of hatred toward God's people across history. The psalm names it so that God's people can bring it to Him instead of carrying it alone.
verses.context: Haman plotted to destroy all the Jews (Esther 3:6). Psalm 83:4 records enemies saying, 'Come, let us wipe them out as a nation.' Yet God preserved a remnant each time.
explore: Meeting places
Local gathering sites for worship and teaching across the land, beyond the central temple in Jerusalem.
Remnant
The surviving portion of God's people whom He preserves through disaster to carry His promises forward.
verses.reflect: How can you pray for believers who are being targeted for their faith today?
verses.alt: Distant columns of smoke rise from several hilltop villages across a valley.

verses.title: No signs, no prophet
verses.heading: Not knowing how long
verses.meaning: Verse 9 may be the loneliest line: 'There are no signs for us to see. There is no longer any prophet. And none of us knows how long this will last.' The people feel cut off from guidance. Nobody can tell them what God is doing or when it will end. Uncertainty can be harder to bear than the suffering itself. The psalm gives permission to admit that we do not know, and still to bring that not-knowing to God.
verses.context: Lamentations 2:9 says 'her prophets find no vision from the LORD.' Amos 8:11 warns of a famine 'of hearing the words of the LORD.' 1 Samuel 3:1 notes that in those days visions were rare.
explore: Signs
Visible tokens of God's presence and care, such as festivals, miracles or messages that reassured His people.
Prophet
A messenger who spoke God's word to the people, often explaining what He was doing in their circumstances.
verses.reflect: What are you waiting on without knowing how long it will last, and how can you rest in God meanwhile?
verses.alt: A lone villager in a head cloth sits on a stone looking at an empty horizon.

verses.title: How long, O God
verses.heading: Taunts against His name
verses.meaning: Verse 10 asks, 'How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You? Will the foe revile Your name forever?' The focus shifts from Israel's suffering to God's reputation. The mocking is aimed at Him. Asaph's deepest concern is that God's name is being dragged through the mud. This is a model for prayer: caring about God's honor more than our own comfort, and asking Him to vindicate His name.
verses.context: 'How long?' is a frequent cry in the Psalms (Psalm 13:1; Psalm 79:5). The martyrs in Revelation 6:10 ask the same. Jesus taught us to pray, 'Hallowed be Your name' (Matthew 6:9).
explore: Taunt
To mock or provoke with insults, often to make someone look weak or foolish in front of others.
Revile
To speak abusively about someone, heaping contempt and scorn on their name and character.
verses.reflect: How might caring about God's name change what you pray for this week?
verses.alt: A lone hillside under heavy clouds with wind bending the grass.

verses.title: Withdrawn right hand
verses.heading: Stretch it out
verses.meaning: Verse 11 pleads, 'Why do You withdraw Your strong right hand? Stretch it out to destroy them!' The picture is of a warrior keeping his hand tucked inside his cloak instead of drawing his sword. Asaph knows God's hand is strong, which is why its stillness is so confusing. He asks God to act as He did at the exodus, when His outstretched arm brought Israel out of Egypt.
verses.context: Exodus 15:6 sings, 'Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power.' Deuteronomy 26:8 recalls 'a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.' Isaiah 59:1 says the LORD's hand is not too short to save.
explore: Right hand
In Scripture a symbol of strength and action; God's right hand stands for His power to save and to judge.
Outstretched arm
An image from the exodus describing God acting openly and powerfully to rescue His people.
verses.reflect: Where are you asking God to stretch out His hand, and what do you know of His strength already?
verses.alt: A strong wind sweeps across a wide plain beneath a breaking sky.

verses.title: My King of old
verses.heading: The hinge of hope
verses.meaning: Verse 12 turns the psalm: 'Yet God is my King from ancient times, working salvation on the earth.' The word 'yet' marks a decision to remember. Nothing has changed outwardly; the temple is still in ruins. But Asaph looks past the present to the long record of God's rule. God was King before this disaster and remains King now. Saving acts across 'the earth' show that He is not limited to one place or moment.
verses.context: Psalm 44:4 says, 'You are my King, O God.' Psalm 93:1 declares, 'The LORD reigns.' Exodus 15:18 ends the song of the sea with 'The LORD will reign forever and ever.'
explore: King from ancient times
God's rule did not begin with Israel's kings; He has reigned since before creation and will reign forever.
Salvation
Rescue and deliverance; in the Psalms it often means God saving His people from enemies and danger.
verses.reflect: What does it mean for you to say 'Yet God is my King' about a hard situation?
verses.alt: Morning sun breaks through clouds over an ancient range of hills.

verses.title: Sea divided
verses.heading: Dragons of the deep
verses.meaning: Verse 13 recalls, 'You divided the sea by Your strength; You smashed the heads of the dragons of the sea.' Asaph points to the Red Sea crossing, when God split the waters for Israel. He also uses poetic language about sea dragons, images other nations used for chaos. The message is that the forces people fear most are no match for God. The God who parted the sea can handle the enemy at the gate.
verses.context: Exodus 14:21 describes the LORD driving back the sea with a strong east wind. Isaiah 51:9–10 also pairs the exodus with God piercing the sea monster. Such images show God as master over all chaos.
explore: Dragons of the sea
Poetic images of chaotic powers in the waters; Scripture uses them to show God's total victory over disorder.
Divided the sea
The exodus miracle in which God opened a dry path through the Red Sea for Israel to escape Egypt.
verses.reflect: Which 'sea' in your life looks impassable, and how does the exodus speak to it?
verses.alt: Tall walls of water stand on either side of a dry seabed path.

verses.title: Leviathan crushed
verses.heading: The monster made food
verses.meaning: Verse 14 continues, 'You crushed the heads of Leviathan; You fed him to the creatures of the desert.' Leviathan was a fearsome sea creature, a symbol of chaos and evil. God not only defeats it but leaves it as food for desert animals, a picture of complete victory. Some readers also hear in it Egypt's army washed up on the shore. Whatever looks monstrous to us is small before God.
verses.context: Job 41:1 asks, 'Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook?' Isaiah 27:1 promises the LORD will slay 'Leviathan the fleeing serpent.' Exodus 14:30 says Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore.
explore: Leviathan
A great sea creature in Hebrew poetry, used as a symbol of chaos and powers opposed to God.
Creatures of the desert
Wild animals and scavengers of the wilderness that feed on what is left behind.
verses.reflect: What fear seems monstrous to you, and how does God's power over Leviathan reframe it?
verses.alt: Waves crash against rocky cliffs under a dramatic dark sky.

verses.title: Fountain and flood
verses.heading: Water opened and dried
verses.meaning: Verse 15 says, 'You broke open the fountain and the flood; You dried up the ever-flowing rivers.' God brought water from the rock in the wilderness, and He dried the Jordan so Israel could cross into the land. He can open water where there is none and stop rivers that never stop. Both acts served His people's needs. The God who controls water controls the circumstances of life.
verses.context: Exodus 17:6 tells of water from the rock at Horeb. Joshua 3:16 records the Jordan's waters stopping. Psalm 105:41 recalls, 'He opened the rock, and water gushed out.'
explore: Fountain
A spring bursting from the ground; here likely recalling the water God brought out of the rock in the wilderness.
Ever-flowing rivers
Rivers that normally never run dry, like the Jordan, which God stopped so Israel could cross.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God to open a spring, or to stop a flood, for you?
verses.alt: Clear water gushes from a crack in a desert rock face.

verses.title: Day and night
verses.heading: Sun and moon in place
verses.meaning: Verse 16 widens the view to creation: 'The day is Yours, and also the night; You established the moon and the sun.' Every hour belongs to God, the bright ones and the dark ones. For people living through a dark season, this is a comfort: the night is His too. He set the lights in the sky, and they still keep their courses. His faithfulness in creation hints at His faithfulness to His people.
verses.context: Genesis 1:16 says God made 'the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night.' Jeremiah 33:20–21 ties God's covenant to the day and night. Psalm 139:12 says darkness is as light to Him.
explore: Established
Set firmly in place; God fixed the sun and moon so that they keep their regular courses.
Covenant with day and night
A promise in Jeremiah that God's faithfulness to His people is as reliable as the cycle of days.
verses.reflect: How does knowing the night belongs to God help you in a dark season?
verses.alt: A pale moon rises over hills while the sun sets on the far side.

verses.title: Summer and winter
verses.heading: Boundaries of the earth
verses.meaning: Verse 17 adds, 'You set all the boundaries of the earth; You made the summer and winter.' God drew the coastlines and arranged the seasons. The seasons keep turning, whatever happens in human history. Asaph reminds himself that the present 'winter' for Israel is held within God's order. Seasons change. The God who made summer can bring it back after a long winter.
verses.context: Genesis 8:22 promises that 'seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter' will not cease. Acts 17:26 says God determined the boundaries of the nations. Ecclesiastes 3:1 says there is a season for everything.
explore: Boundaries
Limits set by God for land and sea and for nations, showing His ordering of the whole world.
Seasons
The yearly cycle of warmth and cold that God promised Noah would continue as long as the earth endures.
verses.reflect: What season are you in right now, and what does God's control of the seasons say to you?
verses.alt: A field half green and half frosted shows summer meeting winter.

verses.title: A foolish people
verses.heading: Remember the mockery
verses.meaning: Verse 18 returns to petition: 'Remember how the enemy has mocked You, O LORD, how a foolish people has spurned Your name.' In Scripture a 'fool' is not someone lacking intelligence but someone who lives as if God does not matter. Asaph asks God to remember, not because God forgets, but as a way of laying the case before Him. Prayer often sounds like this: calling God to act according to who He is.
verses.context: Psalm 14:1 says, 'The fool says in his heart, “There is no God.”' Deuteronomy 32:21 speaks of 'a foolish nation.' Proverbs 1:7 says fools despise wisdom and instruction.
explore: Fool
In biblical language, a person who rejects God and His ways, living morally rather than intellectually foolish.
Spurn
To reject with contempt, refusing to give honor or respect where it is due.
verses.reflect: How can you bring the world's contempt for God to Him in prayer rather than in anger?
verses.alt: A crowd of distant figures stands on a ridge silhouetted against a red sky.

verses.title: Your dove
verses.heading: Do not forget the afflicted
verses.meaning: Verse 19 is tender: 'Do not deliver the soul of Your dove to beasts; do not forget the lives of Your afflicted forever.' Israel calls itself God's dove, gentle, defenseless and loved. The enemies are wild beasts. The prayer is that God will not hand His fragile people over to predators. It shows that God's people can approach Him in weakness, trusting His love for the vulnerable.
verses.context: Song of Solomon 2:14 uses 'my dove' as a term of love. Hosea 7:11 compares Israel to a dove. Jesus told His disciples to be 'innocent as doves' (Matthew 10:16).
explore: Dove
A gentle, defenseless bird; used in Scripture as a term of affection for God's beloved people.
Afflicted
People pressed down by suffering or oppression, whom God repeatedly promises to see and care for.
verses.reflect: In what way do you feel like a defenseless dove, and how can you trust God's care?
verses.alt: A white dove perches on a broken wall near a dark forest edge.

verses.title: Consider the covenant
verses.heading: Dark places of violence
verses.meaning: Verse 20 urges, 'Consider Your covenant, for haunts of violence fill the dark places of the land.' Asaph appeals to God's binding promises to Abraham and Israel. Meanwhile, violence lurks in hidden corners. The strongest argument in prayer is not our goodness but God's covenant faithfulness. He has bound Himself by His word, and His people can hold Him to it.
verses.context: Genesis 17:7 records God's everlasting covenant with Abraham. Leviticus 26:44–45 promises God will not reject His people even in exile. Luke 1:72 celebrates God remembering His holy covenant.
explore: Covenant
A binding agreement; God's covenant with Israel was His committed promise to be their God and keep them.
Haunts of violence
Hidden places where robbers and oppressors lurk, making the land unsafe for ordinary people.
verses.reflect: Which of God's promises can you lean on as you pray about the dark places around you?
verses.alt: A narrow mountain path winds into shadowed rocky ravines.

verses.title: The poor shall praise
verses.heading: Not retreating in shame
verses.meaning: Verse 21 asks, 'Do not let the oppressed retreat in shame; may the poor and needy praise Your name.' Asaph wants the humiliated to have reason to sing. God's rescue of the weak becomes a cause for praise. The goal of deliverance is not just relief but worship. When God lifts up the lowly, they become witnesses to His goodness.
verses.context: Psalm 72:12 says the king 'will deliver the needy who cry out.' Luke 1:52 says God 'has exalted the humble.' Psalm 34:6 says, 'This poor man called out, and the LORD heard him.'
explore: Oppressed
People crushed under unjust power, whom God's law and prophets repeatedly command His people to protect.
Shame
The humiliation of defeat or rejection; God promises that those who trust Him will not be put to shame.
verses.reflect: Who around you feels shamed or crushed, and how could you help them find reason to praise?
verses.alt: A family of villagers walks up a sunny road toward a hilltop.

verses.title: Rise up, O God
verses.heading: Defend Your cause
verses.meaning: Verse 22 cries out, 'Rise up, O God; defend Your cause! Remember how the fool mocks You all day long.' Israel's cause is God's cause. Asaph asks God to stand up like a judge rising from His seat to deliver a verdict. The mockery is constant, 'all day long.' The cry 'Rise up' echoes the prayer Moses spoke whenever the ark set out, asking God to scatter His enemies.
verses.context: Numbers 10:35 records Moses saying, 'Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered.' Psalm 68:1 begins the same way. Psalm 82:8 cries, 'Arise, O God, judge the earth.'
explore: Rise up
A call for God to act decisively, like a judge standing to give a ruling or a warrior rising for battle.
Your cause
God's own case or purpose in the world, which the psalmist sees as bound up with the fate of His people.
verses.reflect: What cause in your life do you believe is really God's, and how will you pray for Him to rise?
verses.alt: Storm clouds part as sunlight streams down on a ruined hill.

verses.title: Do not disregard
verses.heading: An uproar that keeps rising
verses.meaning: The final verse ends without resolution: 'Do not disregard the clamor of Your adversaries, the uproar of Your enemies that ascends continually.' There is no happy ending here, only a final plea. The noise of the enemy keeps rising toward heaven. Asaph trusts that God hears that noise too. Some prayers end in the middle of the struggle, and Scripture includes them so that we know God is not offended by an unfinished lament.
verses.context: Psalm 88 also ends in darkness. Genesis 18:20–21 says the outcry against Sodom reached God. James 5:4 says the cries of the oppressed reach the ears of the Lord.
explore: Clamor
A loud, confused noise of shouting; here the arrogant noise of God's enemies rising up continually.
Unresolved lament
A prayer of sorrow that ends without a clear answer, trusting God while still waiting for His response.
verses.reflect: Are you able to leave a prayer with God even when it feels unfinished?
verses.alt: Smoke still rises over ruins as evening falls on a quiet valley.
